title: DIA-CIM: A Dynamic Iterative Aggregation Graph Neural Network and Its Hardware Co-Design for Energy-Efficient Graph Processing
evidence_span: DIA-CIM co-designs a 28 nm compute-in-memory macro for dynamic-iterative graph aggregation, using CSR-driven output-stationary dataflow, local partial sums, streamed edges, and a sparsity-priority BF16 pipeline; the official description reports 60.01 TFLOPS/W, over 3.56x lower energy, and over 2.32x lower latency on representative DIA workloads.
problem: Dynamic-iterative GNN aggregation improves receptive field per operation but creates serial dependencies and irregular sparse traffic that undermine conventional SIMD accelerators.
method_or_artifact: 28 nm CIM macro with CSR-driven output-stationary dataflow, streamed edge processing, local partial sums, and bit/value-sparsity-aware BF16 pipeline.
workload_or_benchmark: Dynamic-iterative graph neural-network workloads; graph datasets, node/edge sizes, accuracy, and baseline accelerator configurations are unspecified.
hardware_or_process_assumptions: Fabricated 28 nm CMOS compute-in-memory macro; array, ADC/DAC, memory technology, clock, area, and measurement boundary are unspecified.
limits: The description omits graph suite, accuracy, operation counting, macro area, peripheral power, and baseline normalization.
Serial DIA dependencies and sparse traffic may limit utilization outside representative workloads.
Official description only; silicon and application claims require paper-level verification.

title: Leveraging Invariants for Scalable Verification of RISC-V Cryptography Extensions
evidence_span: The work formally verifies the open-source Marian implementation of RISC-V vector cryptography extensions using proof modularization and systematic invariant identification, achieving an additional 174% speedup; it also verifies a second custom implementation and finds a specification violation that prompted an update.
problem: Exhaustive formal verification of wide RISC-V vector cryptography hardware is difficult, despite its security importance.
method_or_artifact: Unbounded modular proofs and invariant-identification methodology focused on counters, handshakes, bounds, and directions.
workload_or_benchmark: Marian and a second custom RISC-V vector-cryptography implementation; proof properties, hardware size, solver, and baseline proof time are unspecified.
hardware_or_process_assumptions: Open-source vector cryptography RTL implementations; bit widths, formal engines, abstraction assumptions, and hardware process are unspecified.
limits: The description omits proof-property count, solver settings, wall-clock baselines, completeness boundaries, and details of the specification flaw.
Speedup is sensitive to invariant selection and formal-engine configuration.
Official description only; proof artifacts and security interpretation require paper-level verification.

title: Safegen: LLM-Driven Assertion Generation and Fault Criticality Evaluation for Functional Safety
evidence_span: SafeGen uses an LLM and Hyper Knowledge Graph to extract verifiable safety specifications, extends the graph with RTL information to generate functional-safety assertions, maps gate-level stuck-at and bridging faults to RTL, and grades criticality with formal verification; a digital-physical field-oriented-control co-simulation validates the flow, with no numeric results supplied.
problem: Simulation-based fault analysis can overestimate criticality and miss semantic safety importance, motivating formal, specification-aware assessment.
method_or_artifact: LLM/HyperKG specification extraction, RTL-guided assertion generation, gate-to-RTL fault mapping, and formal criticality grading.
workload_or_benchmark: Field-oriented-control digital/physical co-simulation; RTL design, fault set, safety requirements, and evaluation metrics are unspecified.
hardware_or_process_assumptions: RTL and gate-level fault models with digital-physical co-simulation; process, controller hardware, simulator, and formal tool are unspecified.
metrics: Semantic-level fault criticality grading demonstrated qualitatively
limits: No assertion pass rates, fault-coverage values, criticality correlation, model/tool configuration, or runtime are supplied.
LLM-extracted specifications and fault mappings may encode domain assumptions or omissions.
Official description only; functional-safety validity requires paper-level verification.

title: GREEN: Towards Scalable Energy-Efficient Workload Scheduling and Placement in the Cloud
evidence_span: GREEN formulates cloud scheduling and placement as graph optimization and uses a graph neural network with reinforcement learning to generate energy-efficient assignments at scale; COSCO simulations and CloudLab experiments report up to 2.17x energy savings over prior resource managers without compromising SLO metrics, with similar solution quality from 100 to 1000 servers in simulation.
problem: Cloud systems are heterogeneous, dynamic, and energy-hungry; heuristic managers scale but are less energy-efficient, while existing ML managers may not scale.
method_or_artifact: GNN-RL cloud resource manager for graph-based workload scheduling and placement.
workload_or_benchmark: COSCO cloud simulations and real-world CloudLab experiments; workloads, server types, SLO definitions, energy measurement, and prior-manager configurations are unspecified.
hardware_or_process_assumptions: Cloud systems ranging from 100 to 1000 servers with heterogeneous resources; server hardware, network, power model, and placement constraints are unspecified.
metrics: No compromise in SLO metrics claimed
Similar solution quality at 100–1000 servers in COSCO
limits: The description omits workload traces, power model, SLO targets, training cost, server heterogeneity, and baseline tuning.
Simulation scale and CloudLab experiments may not share the same energy and SLO conditions.
Official description only; cloud-system and energy claims require paper-level verification.

title: SpecANNS: Accelerating Graph-Based Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search with Speculative In-Storage Computing
evidence_span: SpecANNS uses in-storage FPGAs in a computational-storage device to compute distances, speculatively identifies pages likely to be accessed in later graph-search hops, and exploits NAND flash parallelism; the official description says it reduces query latency and improves energy efficiency on real CSD hardware but gives no numeric results.
problem: Disk-based graph ANNS is dominated by random-node I/O latency, reported as over 90% of search time.
method_or_artifact: Speculative page prediction, in-storage FPGA distance computation, and NAND-parallel page access through a simple CSD interface.
workload_or_benchmark: Disk-based graph approximate nearest-neighbor search; datasets, graph index, recall target, query rate, CSD hardware, and baseline systems are unspecified.
hardware_or_process_assumptions: Real computational-storage device with NAND flash and in-storage FPGA; flash geometry, FPGA resources, interface, and host system are unspecified.
metrics: Random-node I/O reported as over 90% of search time
limits: No latency, energy, recall, dataset, flash, or FPGA values are supplied.
Speculative page selection may trade off extra reads, recall, and storage wear.
Official description only; CSD results require hardware and workload verification.
